title: Can Asking for Help Be a Favor?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes agreeing, at the last minute, to speak to a small student club after school even though he had a backlog of writing and email. He left the hour-long visit feeling energized, and that momentum carried into the overdue writing. The experience reminded him of a survey study of more than 2,000 people showing that we avoid asking for help because we underestimate how willing others are to help, how good helpers feel afterward, and how inconvenienced they are. His own visit matched all three findings: he was willing, he felt better for having helped, and he suffered no inconvenience. Stuart notes that 2026 has been a year of asking for far more help than before, and that the research has held up in practice. The short note closes with a simple encouragement to teachers who are bottling up a need: ask anyway.
points: People systematically underestimate others' willingness to help, so the fear of imposing is usually miscalibrated.
Helpers tend to feel more positive after helping than askers expect, which means a request can function as a favor to the person asked.
Helpers also feel less inconvenienced than askers predict, removing the main reason teachers hold back.
Stuart's own club visit shows how a small act of service can create momentum that unlocks stalled work.
The practical takeaway for educators is to ask for the help you need now rather than waiting until the need becomes a burden.
quotes: It reminded me of the study where researchers found that people tend to avoid asking for help because they underestimate the degree to which people tend to enjoy performing acts of kindness.
It was only an hour, but man… I left feeling GREAT. And that great feeling ended up creating a momentum within me that fueled some of that writing that had become overdue.
I felt a remarkable increase in positive feelings from having helped and was, in fact, helped myself.
For me, 2026 has been a year of asking for a LOT more help than I have before.
Again and again, I find that what the researchers found in their study is true: folks are willing, they express positive emotion in helping, and they don’t seem to regret the help they give.
All of which is to say, if you need help right now, but you’re bottling up that need and not asking for fear of inconveniencing someone…maybe just ask anyways.
